newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Signals mixed ahead of full APEC finance meet.
newsitem.headline: Signals mixed ahead of full APEC finance meet.

text.p: Asia-Pacific financial officials' efforts to forge common standards for markets and capital flows in the region were meeting with mixed success, delegates and officials said on Friday.

Finance ministers of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum are meeting here this weekend, charged with making regulations more uniform and transparent, luring more investment into the region and promoting freer capital flows.
But a senior Asian Development Bank (ADB) official said APEC economies would pursue different paces in liberalising capital markets.

"Some of the east Asian economies felt it very important that they have what you will call the deepening of the financial sector first, before they open up to freer movement of capital," Paul Dickie, the bank's director for infrastructure, energy and financial sectors told reporters.
"They want to make sure that the domestic financial system is fully responsive to market changes and is soundly based...before they open the capital account."

Meeting delegates attending an outdoor dinner at a luxury resort hotel on Friday evening cited proposals for more uniform legal standards on tax treatment across countries and on international capital flows as one of the areas where agreement was lacking.

"The private sector is moving much faster than the governments" in pushing market liberalisation and changes to facilitate capital flows, one Asian delegate told Reuters. "Being a consensus-building forum we don't expect the governments to move as fast as what the private sector wants."

But other delegates said they had been surprised by the pragmatic approach at meetings on Friday, ahead of the full ministerial meeting on Saturday, with participants showing a sense of urgency toward developing regional bond markets and building infrstructure.

The ADB's Dickie said deputy finance ministers had been willing to compromise enough to agree on basic principles promoting a sound macroeconomic environment, a stable and transparent legal and regulatory system, and sectoral policies promoting competition and availability of long-term capital.
But they had not gone beyond agreeing that these were desirable objectives, he said.

Earlier on Friday, meeting host and chair the Philippines said "a set of voluntary principles is expected to be endorsed" by APEC's top financial officials, including initiatives on international regulatory cooperation.

Among them, the government statement said, were: "Anti-money laundering efforts; enhanced cooperation among export credit agencies; strengthening clearing and settlement systems; (and) ratings support for capital market development."

The 18-member APEC comprises Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
